claim: Meningeal enhancement with post-contrast fluid attenuated inversion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be seen in 50% of patients with mild TBIs and no apparent parenchymal damage.
source: Meningeal enhancement with post-contrast fluid attenuated inversion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be seen in 50% of patients with mild TBIs and no apparent parenchymal damage (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roth et al., 2014, which provides external evidence for the statement.

claim: Meningeal enhancement occurs within minutes of injury.
source: This enhancement has been shown to occur within minutes of injury (Turtzo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turtzo et al., 2020.

claim: Many individuals who experienced mild TBIs exhibited extravasation of contrast into the sub-arachnoid space, indicating that the blood-brain-barrier was compromised.
source: Moreover, many individuals who experienced mild TBIs still exhibited extravasation of contrast into the sub-arachnoid space, indicating that the blood-brain-barrier was compromised (Turtzo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turtzo et al., 2020.

claim: Most patients experienced resolution in meningeal enhancement 19 days after injury.
source: While most patients experienced resolution in meningeal enhancement 19 days after injury, about 15% had persistent enhancement three months post-injury, indicating that some patients experienced prolonged periods without complete meningeal repair following mild TBI (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2018.

claim: About 15% of patients had persistent meningeal enhancement three months post-injury.
source: While most patients experienced resolution in meningeal enhancement 19 days after injury, about 15% had persistent enhancement three months post-injury, indicating that some patients experienced prolonged periods without complete meningeal repair following mild TBI (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2018.

claim: The meninges contain lymphatic vessels that drain molecules and cells to peripheral lymph nodes.
source: In addition to housing lymphatic vessels that drain molecules and cells to peripheral lymph nodes (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015), the meninges also contain a full array of innate and adaptive immune cells that are in constant communication with neurons and glia (Alves de Lima et al., 2020b; Alves de Lima et al., 2020a; Rustenhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aspelund et al., 2015 and Louveau et al., 2015.

claim: The meninges contain a full array of innate and adaptive immune cells that are in constant communication with neurons and glia.
source: In addition to housing lymphatic vessels that drain molecules and cells to peripheral lymph nodes (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015), the meninges also contain a full array of innate and adaptive immune cells that are in constant communication with neurons and glia (Alves de Lima et al., 2020b; Alves de Lima et al., 2020a; Rustenhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alves de Lima et al., 2020b; Alves de Lima et al., 2020a; and Rustenhoven et al., 2021.

claim: IFN-γ is important in maintaining social behavior networks.
source: For instance, IFN-γ is important in maintaining social behavior networks, whereas IL-4 production by meningeal T cells has been shown to influence learning and memory (Filiano et al., 2016; Derecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Filiano et al., 2016 and Derecki et al., 2010.

claim: IL-4 production by meningeal T cells has been shown to influence learning and memory.
source: For instance, IFN-γ is important in maintaining social behavior networks, whereas IL-4 production by meningeal T cells has been shown to influence learning and memory (Filiano et al., 2016; Derecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Filiano et al., 2016 and Derecki et al., 2010.

claim: IL-17a secretion by γδ T cells in the meninges can impact anxiety-like behaviors and memory.
source: Recent studies also suggest that IL-17a secretion by γδ T cells in the meninges can impact anxiety-like behaviors and memory (Alves de Lima et al., 2020a; Ribeiro et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alves de Lima et al., 2020a and Ribeiro et al., 2019.

claim: An age-related decline of CCR7 expression by meningeal T cells may contribute to cognitive impairment, brain inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease.
source: Of particular relevance, recent work has shown that an age-related decline of CCR7 expression by meningeal T cells may contribute to cognitive impairment, brain inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease (Da Mesquita et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Da Mesquita et al., 2021.

claim: Male C57BL/6 J wild-type mice at 10 weeks of age were subjected to a mild closed-skull injury above the right inferior temporal lobe or Sham procedure, and one week later, the meninges from 5 mice per group were harvested, pooled, and processed for scRNA-seq.
source: Male C57BL/6 J wild-type (WT) mice at 10 weeks of age were subjected to a mild closed-skull injury above the right inferior temporal lobe or Sham procedure. One week later, the meninges from 5 mice per group were harvested, pooled, and processed for scRNA-seq.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a showing the experimental schematic.

claim: Joint clustering of both the Sham and TBI meninges revealed 21 unique cell populations including endothelial cells, fibroblasts, Schwann cells, and ciliated ependymal cells from the pia.
source: Joint clustering of both the Sham and TBI meninges revealed 21 unique cell populations including endothelial cells, fibroblasts, Schwann cells, and ciliated ependymal cells from the pia (Figure 1b and c, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b, 1c, and Table 1.

claim: The meninges contained a full repertoire of immune cells including macrophages, B cells, T cells, NK cells, dendritic cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and neutrophils.
source: Additionally, the meninges contained a full repertoire of immune cells including macrophages, B cells, T cells, NK cells, dendritic cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and neutrophils (Figure 1b and c, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b, 1c, and Table 1.

claim: Following brain injury, there was a higher frequency of 'Activated Macrophages 1' which exhibit high expression of complement-related genes.
source: Following brain injury, there was a higher frequency of one group of macrophages which we denoted as 'Activated Macrophages 1' as they exhibit high expression of complement-related genes (Figure 1c and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and 1e.

claim: The frequency of fibroblasts was substantially increased following head trauma.
source: Moreover, the frequency of fibroblasts was substantially increased following head trauma (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis of the 'Activated Macrophage' populations revealed 321 upregulated genes and 369 downregulated genes following head injury when using a false discovery rate of <0.1.
source: Differential gene expression analysis of the 'Activated Macrophage' populations (Activated Macrophages 1 & 2) revealed 321 upregulated genes and 369 downregulated genes following head injury when using a false discovery rate of <0.1 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Network analysis on the significantly upregulated genes from activated macrophage populations found an enrichment of pathways related to immune system activation.
source: When we performed a network analysis on the significantly upregulated genes from these populations, we found an enrichment of pathways related to immune system activation (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Some of the most significantly upregulated genes contributing to the immune-related GO terms were important for the type I IFN response including Ifnar1, Ifi203, Irf2bp2, and Irf5.
source: We also noticed that some of the most significantly upregulated genes contributing to the immune-related GO terms were important for the type I IFN response including Ifnar1, Ifi203, Irf2bp2, and Irf5, amongst others (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Elevated expression of genes including Ifnar1, Irf5, Ifnb1, and Ifi203 was observed in whole meningeal samples one week after injury by qPCR.
source: We next examined type I IFN gene expression by qPCR in whole meningeal samples one week after injury. We observed elevated expression of genes including Ifnar1, Irf5, Ifnb1, and Ifi203, highlighting the strong type I IFN gene signature after TBI that is likely driven by meningeal macrophages (Figure 2e–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e-h.

claim: Re-clustering of the three macrophage populations combined from Sham and TBI meninges yielded six different meningeal macrophage clusters.
source: We re-clustered the three macrophage populations (Activated Macrophages 1 & 2, and Macrophages 3) combined from Sham and TBI meninges, which yielded six different meningeal macrophage clusters (Figure 2i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The largest population of macrophages expressed high levels of ferritin.
source: The largest population of macrophages expressed high levels of ferritin ('Ferritin Expressing') (Figure 2i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: There was an overall relative increase in the 'Anti-Inflammatory' and 'Resolution Phase' macrophages in the TBI group.
source: Interestingly, there was an overall relative increase in the 'Anti-Inflammatory' and 'Resolution Phase' macrophages in the TBI group, indicating that one week after injury, the response of the meningeal macrophages appears to shift towards wound healing and inflammation resolution (Figure 2j and k).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2j and 2k.

claim: There was a relative reduction in the 'Ferritin Expressing' macrophages following injury.
source: There was also a relative reduction in the 'Ferritin Expressing' macrophages following injury (Figure 2j and k).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2j and 2k.

claim: After head injury, the 'Fibroblast' population exhibited 368 activated genes and 320 repressed genes.
source: After head injury, the 'Fibroblast' population exhibited 368 activated genes and 320 repressed genes (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A significant increase in collagen density was observed 1 week after TBI.
source: Consistent with the sequencing results, we observed a significant increase in collagen density 1 week after TBI (Figure 3c, d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c, d, and e.

claim: Disease pathways related to neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease, were some of the most highly upregulated pathways altered in fibroblasts after TBI.
source: Interestingly, disease pathways related to neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease, were some of the most highly upregulated pathways altered in fibroblasts after TBI (Figure 3g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: A majority of the fibroblasts in the meninges were from the dura.
source: As expected, we found that a majority of the fibroblasts in the meninges were from the dura, the thickest layer of the meninges and the layer that is targeted by the method of dissection used in these studies (Alves de Lima et al., 2020b; Rua and McGavern, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Alves de Lima et al., 2020b and Rua and McGavern, 2018.

claim: Several dural fibroblast markers (e.g. Foxc2, Fxyd5) were significantly upregulated following injury.
source: When we looked at the expression level of dural fibroblast genes before and after TBI, we saw that several of the markers (e.g. Foxc2, Fxyd5) were significantly upregulated following injury, and other dural markers, while not expressed at significantly higher levels, were clearly expressed by a higher proportion of total cells (e.g. Alpl, Mgp) (Figure 3i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: 151 genes were upregulated and 286 were downregulated following injury in the T cell population.
source: Overall, 151 genes were upregulated and 286 were downregulated following injury in the T cell population, 102 genes were upregulated and 158 were downregulated following injury in the B cell population, and 183 genes were upregulated and 149 were downregulated following injury in the dendritic cell population (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 102 genes were upregulated and 158 were downregulated following injury in the B cell population.
source: Overall, 151 genes were upregulated and 286 were downregulated following injury in the T cell population, 102 genes were upregulated and 158 were downregulated following injury in the B cell population, and 183 genes were upregulated and 149 were downregulated following injury in the dendritic cell population (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 183 genes were upregulated and 149 were downregulated following injury in the dendritic cell population.
source: Overall, 151 genes were upregulated and 286 were downregulated following injury in the T cell population, 102 genes were upregulated and 158 were downregulated following injury in the B cell population, and 183 genes were upregulated and 149 were downregulated following injury in the dendritic cell population (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Within the T cell subsets, there was a clear CD8+ T cell population and two T helper cell populations: Th2 cells and Th17 cells.
source: We found that within the T cell subsets, there was a clear CD8 +T cell population and two T helper cell populations: Th2 cells and Th17 cells (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Re-clustering of the B cell populations revealed five sub-clusters.
source: Re-clustering of the B cell populations revealed five sub-clusters (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The T cell populations did not demonstrate a strong trajectory in their differentiation status.
source: The T cell populations did not demonstrate a strong trajectory in their differentiation status, which is expected given that the populations we identified (Th2, Th17, CD8 + T cells) are all relatively advanced within T cell maturation (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and inference about T cell maturation.

claim: The B cells earliest in the differentiation trajectory were the 'Immature B Cells' and 'Proliferating Cells' populations, whereas the 'Activated B Cells' and 'Mature B cells' were the furthest along in the differentiation trajectory.
source: We observed that the B cells earliest in the differentiation trajectory, as demonstrated by the lowest values on the pseudotime scale, were the 'Immature B Cells' and 'Proliferating Cells' populations, whereas the 'Activated B Cells', that are likely producing antibodies, and 'Mature B cells' were the furthest along in the differentiation trajectory (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The T cell populations upregulated many genes important for survival, activation, cytokine signaling, and antigen recognition.
source: The T cell populations upregulated many genes important for survival (Gimap1, Gimap6), activation (Arrb2, Ppia, Cd48), cytokine signaling (Mif, Il2rg), and antigen recognition (Cd247), all of which contributed to an overall increase in inflammatory response gene expression (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The T cells also upregulated various genes that are known to be involved in the dampening of immune responses such as Socs1 and Cd52.
source: Concomitantly, the T cells also upregulated various genes that are known to be involved in the dampening of immune responses such as Socs1 (Suppressor of Cytokine Signaling-1) and Cd52 (Figure 4f; Liau et al., 2018; Toh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f and citations to Liau et al., 2018 and Toh et al., 2013.

claim: Many upregulated genes in the B cell populations following injury fell into the category of 'B Cell Maturation', including Cd83, Ube2d3, and Doc3.
source: Investigating the genes that were upregulated in the B cell populations following injury, we found that many of these genes fell into the category of 'B Cell Maturation', including Cd83, Ube2d3, and Doc3 (Figure 4g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Of all macrophage ligands, Tgfb1 best predicted the gene expression patterns seen in other cell populations.
source: Of all macrophage ligands, Tgfb1 best predicted the gene expression patterns seen in other cell populations, suggesting the observed transcriptional dynamics reflect an environment of cell growth, differentiation, and alternative macrophage activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b; Gong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b, and a citation to Gong et al., 2012.

claim: Tgfb1 signaling is predicted to activate multiple genes that affect collagen production including Col1a1, Col1a2 and Col3a1.
source: For example, Tgfb1 signaling is predicted to activate multiple genes that affect collagen production including Col1a1, Col1a2 and Col3a1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), aligning with our finding of increased collagen production following TBI (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c and Figure 3c-e.

claim: Many top fibroblast ligands were essential for promoting angiogenesis (Vegfa, Cxcl12, Pgf), growth and inflammation (Apoe, Csf1, Cxcl12, Tgfb3), and extracellular matrix development and wound healing (Col4a1, Hspg2, Nov).
source: More specifically, many top ligands were essential for promoting angiogenesis (Vegfa, Cxcl12, Pgf), growth and inflammation (Apoe, Csf1, Cxcl12, Tgfb3), and extracellular matrix development and wound healing (Col4a1, Hspg2, Nov) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Solé-Boldo et al., 2020; Buechler et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b, and citations to Solé-Boldo et al., 2020; Buechler et al., 2021; and Lin et al., 2005.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that age was the main driver of differential gene expression in the bulk RNA-seq dataset.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that age was the main driver of differential gene expression, as young and aged groups clustered furthest apart (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: While the young mice that had received either Sham or TBI clustered together in the PCA plot, the aged Sham and TBI mice clustered further apart.
source: However, while the young mice that had received either Sham or TBI clustered together in the PCA plot, the aged Sham and TBI mice clustered further apart, indicating that the effects from TBI may have more long-lasting effects on gene expression in aged mice when compared to young mice (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There were only a total of 22 differentially expressed genes when comparing Young Sham with Young TBI.
source: Indeed, when we looked at the number of differentially expressed genes between all four experimental groups, we saw that there were only a total of 22 differentially expressed genes when comparing Young Sham with Young TBI, while there were a total of 364 differentially expressed genes when comparing Aged Sham with Aged TBI (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: There were a total of 364 differentially expressed genes when comparing Aged Sham with Aged TBI.
source: Indeed, when we looked at the number of differentially expressed genes between all four experimental groups, we saw that there were only a total of 22 differentially expressed genes when comparing Young Sham with Young TBI, while there were a total of 364 differentially expressed genes when comparing Aged Sham with Aged TBI (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: 1772 differentially expressed genes were identified when comparing Young Sham mice with Aged Sham mice.
source: Interestingly, 1772 differentially expressed genes were identified when comparing Young Sham mice with Aged Sham mice, and 2936 differentially regulated genes were identified when comparing Young TBI mice with Aged TBI mice (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: 2936 differentially regulated genes were identified when comparing Young TBI mice with Aged TBI mice.
source: Interestingly, 1772 differentially expressed genes were identified when comparing Young Sham mice with Aged Sham mice, and 2936 differentially regulated genes were identified when comparing Young TBI mice with Aged TBI mice (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: There were 917 downregulated genes and 639 upregulated genes that were unique to the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI comparison and not shared with any other comparison.
source: Interestingly, there were 917 downregulated genes and 639 upregulated genes that were unique to the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI comparison and not shared with any other comparison, including the Young Sham vs. Aged Sham comparison.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: There were 595 downregulated genes and 592 upregulated genes that were shared between the Young Sham vs. Aged Sham and Young TBI vs. Aged TBI comparisons.
source: There were 595 downregulated genes and 592 upregulated genes that were shared between these two comparisons, indicating that while a portion of the transcription changes seen in the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI group may be attributed to aging, a significant number of the affected genes were uniquely identified in the setting of trauma in aged mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: One half of the top 20 upregulated genes in the Aged Sham mice as compared to the Young Sham mice were important for antibody production by B cells.
source: Upon examining the top 20 most significantly upregulated and downregulated genes in the Aged Sham mice as compared to the Young Sham mice, we noticed a striking upregulation in genes important for antibody production by B cells (Figure 6a). In fact, one half of the top 20 upregulated genes fell into this category (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Immune and defense responses were among the most highly upregulated GO biological processes in the Young Sham mice versus Aged Sham mice comparison.
source: When we examined the top GO biological processes that were enriched by the significantly activated genes in the Young Sham mice versus Aged Sham mice comparison, we saw that immune and defense responses were among the most highly upregulated (Figure 6b), indicating that the cells within the aged meninges have grossly upregulated their immune response, even in homeostatic conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Highly significant upregulations in genes related to the immunoglobulin heavy chain (Ighm, Ighg2b, Igha), light chain (Igkc), and components of IgA or IgM antibodies (Jchain) were found in aged mice.
source: We found highly significant upregulations in genes related to the immunoglobulin heavy chain (Ighm, Ighg2b, Igha), light chain (Igkc), and components of IgA or IgM antibodies (Jchain) (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Aged meninges have significantly increased J chain deposition that is concentrated along the sinuses.
source: Using immunohistochemistry on meningeal whole mounts, we confirmed that aged meninges have significantly increased J chain deposition that is concentrated along the sinuses (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d and 6e.

claim: The number of cells expressing B220 along the meningeal transverse sinus in mice was significantly lower in aged mice.
source: Interestingly, we saw that the number cells expressing B220 along the meningeal transverse sinus in mice was significantly lower in aged mice (Figure 6f and g), which is in contrast to other recent studies have shown that B cells comprise a larger proportion and number of cells in aged dural meninges (Brioschi et al., 2021; Mrdjen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f and 6g, and contrasted with citations to Brioschi et al., 2021 and Mrdjen et al., 2018.

claim: The aged dural meninges had overall fewer cells when compared to young dural meninges.
source: The aged dural meninges had overall fewer cells when compared to young dural meninges (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Upon examination of total B220+, CD19+, and B220+CD19+ cell numbers, no significant differences were seen in aged mice.
source: Upon examination of total B220+, CD19+, and B220 + CD19 + cell numbers, we did not see significant differences in aged mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Increased expression of type I interferon (IFN)-related genes was observed within the bulk RNA sequencing dataset in aged mice.
source: In addition to the antibody-related gene upregulation, we also observed increased expression of type I interferon (IFN)-related genes within the bulk RNA sequencing dataset (Figure 6h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Highly significant increases in type I IFN related genes including Ifit1, Ifit2, Irf7, Ifi213, and Mx1 were seen in aged mice.
source: Amongst others, we saw highly significant increases in type I IFN related genes including Ifit1, Ifit2, Irf7, Ifi213, and Mx1 (Figure 6h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Many repressed genes unique to the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI comparison are involved in binding processes, including protein binding and cytoskeletal binding.
source: Using GO molecular function terms, we saw that of the repressed genes unique to the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI comparison, many of these genes are involved in binding processes, including protein binding and cytoskeletal binding (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Many of the top repressed genes unique to the Aged TBI versus Young TBI comparison encode for collagenases (Col4a1, Col4a2, and Col5a2) and other molecules involved in regulating cellular junctions (Jup).
source: When we looked more closely at the top repressed genes unique to the Aged TBI versus Young TBI comparison, we observed that many of these genes encode for collagenases (Col4a1, Col4a2, and Col5a2) and other molecules involved in regulating cellular junctions (Jup) (Figure 7b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Some genes important for collagenase production were downregulated in aged mice 1.5 months after TBI in the dural meninges as validated by qPCR.
source: Using qPCR, we validated that some of these genes important for collagenase production were indeed downregulated in aged mice 1.5 months after TBI in the dural meninges (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Genes associated with immune activation were profoundly upregulated in aged TBI mice in comparison to their young TBI counterparts.
source: Additionally, we looked into the genes that were uniquely activated in the Aged TBI mice as compared to the Young TBI mice. We found that genes associated with immune activation were profoundly upregulated in aged TBI mice in comparison to their young TBI counterparts (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The most enriched GO biological processes in aged TBI mice included the 'defense response' and 'immune system process'.
source: The most enriched GO biological processes included the 'defense response' and 'immune system process' (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Some of the genes that contributed to the upregulation of immune-related terms in aged TBI mice included those associated with immunoglobulin production (Ighg2c), T and B cell signaling (Cd24a, Zap70, Cxcr6), and cell death (Casp12, C2).
source: Some of the genes that contributed to the upregulation of these immune-related terms included those associated with immunoglobulin production (Ighg2c), T and B cell signaling (Cd24a, Zap70, Cxcr6), and cell death (Casp12, C2) (Figure 7e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: There were 139 shared differentially regulated genes between the T cells, B cells, Fibroblasts, and Macrophages in the scRNA-seq dataset and the Young Sham vs. Aged Sham comparison in the bulk RNA-seq dataset.
source: First, we compared the differentially expressed genes in the T cells, B cells, Fibroblasts, and Macrophages in the scRNA-seq dataset with the differentially expressed genes in the Young Sham vs. Aged Sham comparison, to determine whether some of these genes were shared with aging alone (Figure 8a). While there were 139 shared differentially regulated genes, a majority of the differentially expressed genes in each dataset were not shared (Figure 8a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Many shared downregulated genes between the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets were important for wound healing and maintenance of connective tissue.
source: When we looked more closely at the shared downregulated genes, we found that many were important for wound healing and maintenance of connective tissue (Figure 8c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Some of the upregulated genes that were shared at the subacute time point and chronically in aging were genes that contribute to abnormal immune cell physiology, innate immune response, and immune cell activation.
source: Some of the upregulated genes that were shared at the subacute time point and chronically in aging were genes that contribute to abnormal immune cell physiology, innate immune response, and immune cell activation, again supporting the notion that aged meninges adopt a chronic, baseline activation of the immune system (Figure 8c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: There were 119 genes in common between the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI bulk RNA sequencing comparison and the T cells, B cells, Fibroblasts, and Macrophages of the scRNA-seq dataset.
source: Looking more closely at the differentially regulated genes shared between the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI bulk RNA sequencing comparison and the T cells, B cells, Fibroblasts, and Macrophages of the scRNA-seq dataset, we found 119 genes in common (Figure 8b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Many of the common upregulated genes between the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets were related to abnormal immune cell activation.
source: Similar to aging alone, many of the common upregulated genes were related to abnormal immune cell activation, reflecting the chronically activated immune response that occurs after TBI in aging (Figure 8d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Of the shared downregulated genes between the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets, many contribute to cell adhesion and response to endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: Of the shared downregulated genes, many contribute to cell adhesion and response to endoplasmic reticulum stress (Figure 8d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: The elderly experience more severe consequences than younger individuals with similar injury severity following TBI.
source: While TBI affects individuals of all ages, the elderly experience more severe consequences than younger individuals with similar injury severity (Susman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Susman et al., 2002.

claim: Prolonged activation of the immune system following TBI may contribute to some of the negative TBI-associated sequelae.
source: Multiple findings have indicated that prolonged activation of the immune system following TBI may contribute to some of the negative TBI-associated sequelae (Ertürk et al., 2016; Winston et al., 2016; Corps et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2013; Schimmel et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2018; McKee and Lukens, 2016; Witcher et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several studies point to differences in the immune response in elderly individuals that may contribute to more severe consequences following injury.
source: Interestingly, several studies point to differences in the immune response in elderly individuals that may contribute to more severe consequences following injury (Chou et al., 2018; Morganti et al., 2016; Ritzel et al., 2018; Webster et al., 2015; Androvic et al., 2020; Ritzel et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2013; Krukowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent findings have implicated the meninges as an early responder to TBI and as a pivotal contributor to the CNS immune response following injury.
source: Recent findings have implicated the meninges, a tri-layered tissue that resides between the brain parenchyma and skull, as an early responder to TBI and as a pivotal contributor to the CNS immune response following injury (Russo et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Russo et al., 2018 and Roth et al., 2014.

claim: Studies by Roth et al. demonstrated that the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which occurs as part of meningeal macrophage cell death, can trigger subsequent tissue damage in the brain parenchyma.
source: For instance, studies by Roth et al. demonstrated that the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which occurs as part of meningeal macrophage cell death, can trigger subsequent tissue damage in the brain parenchyma (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roth et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking ROS release by dying meningeal macrophages is effective in minimizing cell death in the brain parenchyma.
source: Interestingly, they showed that blocking ROS release by dying meningeal macrophages is also effective in minimizing cell death in the brain parenchyma.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the cited study by Roth et al., 2014.

claim: Meningeal macrophages play important roles in coordinating meningeal remodeling and vascular repair following mild head trauma.
source: More recently, this same group also demonstrated that meningeal macrophages play important roles in coordinating meningeal remodeling and vascular repair following mild head trauma (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2018.

claim: Distinct macrophage populations function within defined regions in and around the injury site.
source: Here, they showed that distinct macrophage populations function within defined regions in and around the injury site.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the cited study by Russo et al., 2018.

claim: Inflammatory myelomonocytic cells work in the core of the lesion where dead cells are abundant.
source: For example, they identified that inflammatory myelomonocytic cells work in the core of the lesion where dead cells are abundant, whereas wound-healing macrophages are present along the perimeter of the injury where they work to restore blood vasculature and clear fibrin (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2018.

claim: Wound-healing macrophages are present along the perimeter of the injury where they work to restore blood vasculature and clear fibrin.
source: For example, they identified that inflammatory myelomonocytic cells work in the core of the lesion where dead cells are abundant, whereas wound-healing macrophages are present along the perimeter of the injury where they work to restore blood vasculature and clear fibrin (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2018.

claim: Recent studies suggest that elevated type I IFN signaling in the brain parenchyma is a driver of detrimental outcomes in TBI pathogenesis.
source: Interestingly, recent studies suggest that elevated type I IFN signaling in the brain parenchyma is a driver of detrimental outcomes in TBI pathogenesis (Karve et al., 2016; Barrett et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Karve et al., 2016 and Barrett et al., 2020.

claim: IgA-producing plasma B cells survey the meninges and their IgA secretion provides an 'immunological barrier' to prevent potential pathogens from gaining access into the brain parenchyma.
source: Interestingly, emerging studies have proposed that IgA-producing plasma B cells survey the meninges and that their IgA secretion provides an 'immunological barrier' to prevent potential pathogens from gaining access into the brain parenchyma (Fitzpatrick et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fitzpatrick et al., 2020.

claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are known to be potent producers of type I IFNs.
source: Notably, the presence of plasmacytoid dendritic cells within the meninges is intriguing as they are known to be potent producers of type I IFNs (Fitzgerald-Bocarsly et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fitzgerald-Bocarsly et al., 2008.

claim: Sex differences play a role in outcomes after TBI both in human and animal models.
source: It is also known that sex differences play a role in outcomes after TBI both in human and animal models (Gupte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gupte et al., 2019.

claim: Men have a higher likelihood of sustaining a TBI.
source: While men have a higher likelihood of sustaining a TBI, women have a higher likelihood of suffering worse outcomes (Gupte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gupte et al., 2019.

claim: Women have a higher likelihood of suffering worse outcomes after TBI.
source: While men have a higher likelihood of sustaining a TBI, women have a higher likelihood of suffering worse outcomes (Gupte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gupte et al., 2019.

claim: Aged individuals have a higher morbidity and mortality than young individuals when experiencing a similar severity brain injury.
source: It is well known that aged individuals have a higher morbidity and mortality than young individuals when experiencing a similar severity brain injury (Susman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Susman et al., 2002.

claim: Many studies have highlighted baseline changes in the aged brain that has been speculated to prime the elderly for differential responses following injury, including changes in the BBB, microglial dysfunction, and an overall increase in neuroinflammation.
source: Many studies have highlighted baseline changes in the aged brain that has been speculated to prime the elderly for differential responses following injury, including changes in the BBB, microglial dysfunction, and an overall increase in neuroinflammation (Androvic et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Marschallinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Androvic et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; and Marschallinger et al., 2020.

claim: Other findings support changes in the response to injury in the aged brain, including alterations in the type and number of immune cells recruited to the injury site, further increases in inflammatory gene signatures in the brain parenchyma, and elevated production of potentially neurotoxic molecules such as ROS and type I IFNs.
source: Furthermore, other findings support changes in the response to injury in the aged brain, including alterations in the type and number of immune cells recruited to the injury site, further increases in inflammatory gene signatures in the brain parenchyma, and elevated production of potentially neurotoxic molecules such as ROS and type I IFNs (Chou et al., 2018; Morganti et al., 2016; Ritzel et al., 2018; Androvic et al., 2020; Ritzel et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2013; Krukowski et al., 2018; Karve et al., 2016; Barrett et al., 2020; Baruch et al., 2014; Abdullah et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017; Itoh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent studies have implicated the meningeal lymphatic system in modulating inflammation in the brain following TBI and sub-arachnoid hemorrhage.
source: Recent studies have implicated the meningeal lymphatic system, which resides in the dura, in modulating inflammation in the brain following TBI and sub-arachnoid hemorrhage (Bolte et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Pu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bolte et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020; and Pu et al., 2019.

claim: Impairments in the meningeal lymphatic system prior to brain injury result in increased gliosis and worsened behavioral outcomes.
source: In these studies, impairments in the meningeal lymphatic system prior to brain injury were found to result in increased gliosis and worsened behavioral outcomes (Bolte et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bolte et al., 2020 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The meningeal lymphatic system is impaired in aging.
source: Interestingly, the meningeal lymphatic system is also known to be impaired in aging (Da Mesquita et al., 2018; Ahn et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2017), and we have previously shown that the rejuvenation of the meningeal lymphatic vasculature in aged mice dampens the subsequent gliosis following TBI (Bolte et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Da Mesquita et al., 2018; Ahn et al., 2019; and Ma et al., 2017.

claim: The rejuvenation of the meningeal lymphatic vasculature in aged mice dampens the subsequent gliosis following TBI.
source: Interestingly, the meningeal lymphatic system is also known to be impaired in aging (Da Mesquita et al., 2018; Ahn et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2017), and we have previously shown that the rejuvenation of the meningeal lymphatic vasculature in aged mice dampens the subsequent gliosis following TBI (Bolte et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bolte et al., 2020.

claim: Head injury in this TBI model does not result in appreciable alterations in balance, motor coordination, reflex, and alertness.
source: Of note, we have previously shown that head injury in this model does not result in appreciable alterations in balance, motor coordination, reflex, and alertness (Bolte et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bolte et al., 2020.

claim: No appreciable differences in CD31 blood vasculature staining were observed at 24 hr following head trauma.
source: Consistent with the mild nature of this TBI model, we also do not observe any appreciable differences in CD31 blood vasculature staining at 24 hr following head trauma (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: Only modest increases in gliosis (Iba1 and GFAP staining) were detected at 24 hr post-TBI.
source: Moreover, we only detect modest increases in gliosis (Iba1 and GFAP staining) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, e and f) and MHCII + staining in the meninges at 24 hr post-TBI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g, h and i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, e, and f.

claim: MHCII+ staining in the meninges was modestly increased at 24 hr post-TBI.
source: Moreover, we only detect modest increases in gliosis (Iba1 and GFAP staining) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, e and f) and MHCII + staining in the meninges at 24 hr post-TBI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g, h and i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g, h, and i.

claim: The meningeal response to brain injury can be divided into several phases: acute, sub-acute, and chronic.
source: The meningeal response to brain injury can be divided into several phases: acute, sub-acute, and chronic (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roth et al., 2014.

claim: Initial studies of the acute phase response after a mild TBI detail a meningeal response that consists of rapid meningeal cell death due to vascular leakage and reactive oxygen species release, which results in secondary parenchymal damage within the first several hours of injury.
source: Initial studies of the acute phase response after a mild TBI detail a meningeal response that consists of rapid meningeal cell death due to vascular leakage and reactive oxygen species release, which results in secondary parenchymal damage within the first several hours of injury (Russo et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Russo et al., 2018 and Roth et al., 2014.

claim: The initial injury is followed by meningeal neutrophil swarming (present within an hour of injury) that is essential for regeneration of the initially damaged glial limitans.
source: The initial injury is followed by meningeal neutrophil swarming (present within an hour of injury) that is essential for regeneration of the initially damaged glial limitans (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roth et al., 2014.

claim: Disrupted meningeal vasculature is repaired during the week following injury by non-classical monocytes.
source: Disrupted meningeal vasculature is then repaired during the week following injury by non-classical monocytes (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Russo et al., 2018.

claim: Brain interstitial fluid (ISF) and CSF intermix in the subarachnoid space and both recirculate throughout the brain via the glymphatic system and drain through the meningeal lymphatic network to the periphery.
source: Brain interstitial fluid (ISF) and CSF intermix in the subarachnoid space and both recirculate throughout the brain via the glymphatic system and drain through the meningeal lymphatic network to the periphery (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015; Plog et al., 2015; Ringstad and Eide, 2020; Louveau et al., 2017; Goodman and Iliff, 2020; Antila et al., 2017; Iliff et al., 2013; Iliff et al., 2014; Iliff et al., 2012; Jessen et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The glymphatic system provides meningeal cells and cells within the CSF with access to brain antigens and proteins.
source: This system provides meningeal cells and cells within the CSF with access to brain antigens and proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the description of the glymphatic system and its function.

claim: The upregulation of antibody production genes in the meninges may be a protective strategy to counteract the loss of blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity that can occur both in aging and following TBI.
source: While speculative, perhaps this upregulation in antibody production genes in the meninges is a protective strategy that is mobilized to counteract the loss of blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity that can occur both in aging and following TBI (Ren et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the data, with supporting citations to Ren et al., 2013 and Yang et al., 2020.

claim: The meninges may play a role in the differential response to head trauma seen in aging.
source: Our findings indicate that the meninges may also play a role in this differential response to head trauma seen in aging.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The increased baseline type I IFN gene signature and antibody production observed in aging potentially renders the aged brain prone to more severe clinical outcomes post-TBI.
source: In particular, it is possible that the increased baseline type I IFN gene signature and antibody production observed in aging potentially renders the aged brain prone to more severe clinical outcomes post-TBI.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the data.

claim: The meningeal lymphatic impairment in aging may contribute to the overall increase in inflammation seen in the aged meninges.
source: Furthermore, whether the meningeal lymphatic impairment in aging contributes to the overall increase in inflammation seen in the aged meninges is another area for future investigation.
evidence: This claim is speculative and proposed as a hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells could be contributing to the type I IFN signature seen with aging and TBI in the meninges.
source: It is possible that plasmacytoid cells could be contributing to the type I IFN signature seen with aging and TBI in the meninges; however, future work is needed to formally investigate this.
evidence: This claim is speculative and proposed as a hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: The dural compartment likely undergoes an increase in fibroblast cell frequency one week after brain injury.
source: This indicates that the dural compartment likely undergoes an increase in fibroblast cell frequency one week after brain injury, which is also consistent with the increase in collagen density seen in the meninges 1 week after TBI (Figure 3c, d and e).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 3i and Figure 3c, d, and e.

claim: A change in the metabolic state of the fibroblasts may be underlying disease-related processes after TBI.
source: Many of the same terms that contribute to the oxidative phosphorylation KEGG term also contribute to the various disease-related KEGG terms, indicating a change in the metabolic state of the fibroblasts may be underlying disease-related processes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the overlap of genes in KEGG terms.

claim: TBI drives the activation and maturation of B cell populations in the meningeal compartment.
source: The upregulation of these genes suggests that TBI drives the activation and maturation of B cell populations in the meningeal compartment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the upregulation of B cell activation and maturation genes.

claim: The observed transcriptional dynamics reflect an environment of cell growth, differentiation, and alternative macrophage activation.
source: Of all macrophage ligands, Tgfb1 best predicted the gene expression patterns seen in other cell populations, suggesting the observed transcriptional dynamics reflect an environment of cell growth, differentiation, and alternative macrophage activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b; Gong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NicheNet analysis and supported by a citation to Gong et al., 2012.

claim: The predicted ligand-target interactions between the macrophage population and other major meningeal cell populations after brain injury illustrate a proliferative, pro-inflammatory state.
source: Overall, the predicted ligand-target interactions between the macrophage population and other major meningeal cell populations after brain injury illustrate a proliferative, pro-inflammatory state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NicheNet analysis results.

claim: Meningeal fibroblasts likely influence gene expression signatures after TBI to promote pro-growth and angiogenic signaling cascades in addition to a balanced upregulation of the immune system.
source: Altogether, meningeal fibroblasts likely influence gene expression signatures after TBI to promote pro-growth and angiogenic signaling cascades in addition to a balanced upregulation of the immune system.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NicheNet analysis results.

claim: The effects from TBI may have more long-lasting effects on gene expression in aged mice when compared to young mice.
source: However, while the young mice that had received either Sham or TBI clustered together in the PCA plot, the aged Sham and TBI mice clustered further apart, indicating that the effects from TBI may have more long-lasting effects on gene expression in aged mice when compared to young mice (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PCA clustering pattern shown in Figure 5b.

claim: While a portion of the transcription changes seen in the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI group may be attributed to aging, a significant number of the affected genes were uniquely identified in the setting of trauma in aged mice.
source: There were 595 downregulated genes and 592 upregulated genes that were shared between these two comparisons, indicating that while a portion of the transcription changes seen in the Young TBI vs. Aged TBI group may be attributed to aging, a significant number of the affected genes were uniquely identified in the setting of trauma in aged mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of shared and unique differentially expressed genes.

claim: Aging profoundly affects meningeal gene expression.
source: Overall, this indicates that aging profoundly affects meningeal gene expression and that mild head trauma in aging results in even larger changes in gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the large number of differentially expressed genes in aging comparisons.

claim: Mild head trauma in aging results in even larger changes in gene expression than aging alone.
source: Overall, this indicates that aging profoundly affects meningeal gene expression and that mild head trauma in aging results in even larger changes in gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of differentially expressed genes across conditions.

claim: Recovery post-TBI may be delayed with aging.
source: Moreover, while the young mice exhibit very few gene expression changes 1.5 months following TBI, the aged mice experience many more alterations in gene expression that last for a longer period of time, which suggests that recovery post-TBI may be delayed with aging.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential gene expression patterns between young and aged mice at 1.5 months post-TBI.

claim: The cells within the aged meninges have grossly upregulated their immune response, even in homeostatic conditions.
source: When we examined the top GO biological processes that were enriched by the significantly activated genes in the Young Sham mice versus Aged Sham mice comparison, we saw that immune and defense responses were among the most highly upregulated (Figure 6b), indicating that the cells within the aged meninges have grossly upregulated their immune response, even in homeostatic conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The increase in antibody-related gene expression seen in aging may reflect a change in the function of the B cells in the dural meninges rather than a recruitment of more B cells.
source: In summation, we do not see increases in B cell numbers in the aged dura, which suggests that the increase in antibody-related gene expression seen in aging may reflect a change in the function of the B cells in the dural meninges rather than a recruitment of more B cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that antibody gene expression is increased without an increase in B cell numbers.

claim: The composition of the B cell population in aged mice may be substantially different than in young mice.
source: Overall, this suggests that the composition of the B cell population in aged mice may be substantially different than in young mice; however, future studies are needed to formally evaluate this in greater detail.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differences in antibody gene expression and B cell numbers, and is proposed as a hypothesis for future investigation.

claim: Pathways important for the wound healing response of the meninges were upregulated in the response to TBI in young mice but are downregulated after brain injury in aging.
source: These pathways likely aid in the wound healing response of the meninges and were upregulated in the response to TBI in young mice (Figure 3), however are downregulated after brain injury in aging.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of gene expression patterns between young and aged mice after TBI.

claim: Mild TBI in aged mice results in prolonged activation of immune genes and decreased expression of genes involved in extracellular matrix remodeling and the maintenance of cellular junctions.
source: In summary, these findings highlight some of the distinct changes seen in the aged meningeal tissue following TBI. Specifically, we find that mild TBI in aged mice results in prolonged activation of immune genes and decreased expression of genes involved in extracellular matrix remodeling and the maintenance of cellular junctions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential gene expression analysis comparing young and aged mice after TBI.

claim: The meningeal transcriptome in young mice returns almost completely to baseline resting levels by 1.5 months post mild head injury.
source: Furthermore, we report that while the meningeal transcriptome in young mice returns almost completely to baseline resting levels by 1.5 months post mild head injury, the aged meninges, in contrast, continue to exhibit substantial and protracted transcriptional alterations related to head injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the small number of differentially expressed genes in young mice at 1.5 months post-TBI.

claim: The aged meninges continue to exhibit substantial and protracted transcriptional alterations related to head injury at 1.5 months post-TBI.
source: Furthermore, we report that while the meningeal transcriptome in young mice returns almost completely to baseline resting levels by 1.5 months post mild head injury, the aged meninges, in contrast, continue to exhibit substantial and protracted transcriptional alterations related to head injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the large number of differentially expressed genes in aged mice at 1.5 months post-TBI.

claim: Some of the downregulated genes important for wound healing in the subacute time point after TBI remain chronically downregulated in the aged meninges.
source: These data suggest that some of the downregulated genes important for wound healing in the subacute time point after TBI remain chronically downregulated in the aged meninges, further supporting the idea that aged meninges may be less able to respond to injury at baseline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the shared downregulated genes between the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets.

claim: Aged meninges may be less able to respond to injury at baseline.
source: These data suggest that some of the downregulated genes important for wound healing in the subacute time point after TBI remain chronically downregulated in the aged meninges, further supporting the idea that aged meninges may be less able to respond to injury at baseline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the persistent downregulation of wound healing genes in aged meninges.

claim: Aged meninges adopt a chronic, baseline activation of the immune system.
source: Some of the upregulated genes that were shared at the subacute time point and chronically in aging were genes that contribute to abnormal immune cell physiology, innate immune response, and immune cell activation, again supporting the notion that aged meninges adopt a chronic, baseline activation of the immune system (Figure 8c).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the shared upregulated immune-related genes between the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets.

claim: While the young meninges initially upregulate some genes important for an inflammatory response one week following TBI, gene expression levels eventually return to baseline.
source: Alternatively, while the young meninges initially upregulate some genes important for an inflammatory response one week following TBI, gene expression levels eventually return to baseline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of gene expression at 1 week and 1.5 months post-TBI in young mice.

claim: The common genes between the scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets reflect a pattern of abnormal immune cell activation and a defective response to healing.
source: Altogether, while a majority of the genes that were differentially expressed in both the bulk RNA and scRNA sequencing datasets were not shared, the common genes reflect a pattern of abnormal immune cell activation and a defective response to healing as demonstrated by the downregulation of genes important for extracellular matrix repair and cellular adhesion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of shared differentially expressed genes between datasets.

claim: While the aged mice still exhibit the signature of abnormal immune activation and defective wound healing 1.5 months after injury, the young mice express these shared genes initially, but return to baseline levels 1.5 months after injury.
source: While the aged mice still exhibit this signature 1.5 months after injury, the young mice express these shared genes initially, but return to baseline levels 1.5 months after injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal comparison of gene expression patterns between young and aged mice.
